opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most exciting areas right now, and it actually comes quite naturally out of our history at DeepMind. If you think back to AlphaGo, that was already a hybrid system in a sense. You had a neural network that learned a model of the game, an intuition for which moves looked promising and who was winning, and then on top of that you had Monte Carlo tree search, a planning process that could explore and check those intuitions. Neither part alone would have been enough. The network gave you the pattern recognition, and the search gave you the ability to reason forward, try things out, and correct mistakes.

Foundation models are incredibly powerful. They've absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge about the world, language, code, and science, and they're a fantastic general-purpose prior. But on their own they still have weaknesses. They can be inconsistent, they can confabulate, and they don't always do the deep, step-by-step planning or exact reasoning that some problems need. So the question becomes: how do you take that rich learned model and combine it with techniques that are very good at the things it's weaker at?

That might be search and planning, like in the games work. It might be formal verification, which is what we did with AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry, where the language model proposes ideas and a symbolic system checks them rigorously, so you know the answer is correct and not just plausible. It could be tool use, calling out to simulators, solvers, or code execution. In science, with something like AlphaFold, you're combining learned representations with a lot of domain structure and physical constraints.

The appeal is that you get the best of both worlds: the flexibility and breadth of learning plus the precision, reliability, and verifiability of more classical methods. And I think that matters a lot if we want these systems to be genuinely useful for science and for high-stakes applications, where "roughly right" isn't good enough.

There's also a deeper reason. I've always thought of the brain as a kind of existence proof, and the brain isn't one monolithic thing. You have different systems, memory, planning, perception, working together. I suspect AGI will look similar: a powerful core model, the foundation model, surrounded by and interacting with other capabilities like planning, memory, and search. Whether some of those eventually get absorbed into the model itself through learning is an open empirical question, and we're exploring both routes. But right now hybrid approaches let us push the frontier on problems that pure scaling alone hasn't cracked yet, and they teach us a lot about what's still missing.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes from a fairly simple observation, which is that foundation models are extraordinary at some things and quite weak at others. They're incredible at pattern recognition, at compressing the world's knowledge, at generating plausible outputs in domains where we have a lot of data. But they're not naturally good at things like precise reasoning, or search, or verification, or planning over long horizons where every step has to be correct. And those happen to be exactly the things that classical computer science has spent decades getting very good at.

So the obvious question is, why would you throw all that away? AlphaGo is actually a nice example of this. The neural networks gave you intuition, a sense of which moves looked promising and how good a position was. But on their own they weren't superhuman. It was combining them with Monte Carlo tree search, an explicit search procedure, that let the system think, in a sense, and check its intuitions against actual lookahead. And the two together were far stronger than either alone. AlphaFold is similar. There's a lot of structure baked into that architecture about physics and geometry and evolutionary information, it's not just a generic model you pointed at protein sequences.

I think of it a bit like how the brain works, actually. We have fast, intuitive, System 1 type processing, and then we have slower, more deliberate reasoning that we use when the stakes are high or the problem is hard. The foundation model gives you the first part. The question is what you wrap around it, so that when it proposes something, there's a mechanism to search, to verify, to run a simulation, to call a solver, to ground the answer in something real rather than just in what sounds right.

And this matters enormously for science, which is really what I care about most. If you want a system to help discover a new material or a new drug, you can't have it hallucinating. You need its creativity, its ability to generate hypotheses, but you need that coupled to something that checks them against the actual constraints of the world, whether that's a physics simulator or a theorem prover or an experiment. I think that's where we'll see the most reliable and the most useful systems come from, not from scaling one component endlessly, but from getting the architecture of the whole system right.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting thing is that different computational approaches have complementary strengths. Foundation models are very good at learning patterns, bringing together knowledge, and interpreting what you’re asking. But some problems benefit from explicit search, planning, or precise computation.

Take a mathematical problem. You might want a model to suggest a promising approach, then use a symbolic system to check a calculation or verify a step. Or in a planning problem, the model could propose possible actions, and a search procedure could explore their consequences before committing to one.

The interesting question is how tightly you integrate those components. Can the system learn when it needs to think more, when it should use a tool, and when its initial answer is sufficient? I think that combination—rich learned representations with the ability to reason and check things at inference time—is a very promising direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think foundation models are giving us an incredibly powerful way of understanding the world and representing knowledge. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re the best tool for every kind of computation. If you need to do an exact calculation, or search through a very large space of possibilities, we already have techniques that are extremely good at those things.

Games are a useful example. You can have a neural network that gives you an intuition about which moves are promising, and then use search to examine the consequences. The intuition makes the search tractable, and the search lets you go beyond your immediate intuition.

So I think there’s a very interesting direction where a foundation model provides this general understanding, but can also call on tools, planning algorithms, or simulators when it needs to. The hard part is making that combination seamless: knowing when to reason more deeply, which tool to use, and how to check the result. If we get that right, you get a system that’s both more capable and more reliable.
